html:
The first part of the Eastern Zhou era in China, from 770 to about 476 BCE. The Zhou kings still reigned, but real power passed to the lords of dozens of rival states. It is named after the Spring and Autumn Annals, the chronicle of the small state of Lu, which tradition says Confucius edited.

It began when invaders sacked the old Zhou capital in the west, and the court moved east to Luoyang. The king kept his title and rituals, but the great lords made their own wars and alliances. Over three centuries more than a hundred small states were swallowed by a few big ones: Qi in the east, Jin in the north, Chu in the south, Qin in the west. The strongest lord of the day was recognised as hegemon and led the others in the king's name.

Late in the period the southern states of Wu and Yue rose. Yue destroyed Wu in 473 BCE. The general Sun Tzu, author of The Art of War, is said to have served Wu.

Iron tools spread, trade grew, and old noble families lost ground to men of talent. This unsettled world produced China's first great thinkers: Confucius (born 551 BCE) and, by tradition, Laozi. Their ideas, later Confucianism and Daoism, answered the question of how to restore order. The era gave way to the even fiercer Warring States period, when Jin split into three states, one of them Zhao.
